en: The Parivāra:
The Second Part of the Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga.
1.9 Chapter on the Formulation of Rules (Katthapaññattivāra) 1. Section on the Defeats (Pārājikakaṇḍa):

Where was the offense of defeat formulated by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—concerning the practice of sexual intercourse? With reference to whom? On account of what matter? ... [as above] ...
By whom was it brought forth?

That which was made a *pārājika* offense by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—on account of engaging in sexual intercourse: where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Vesālī.
With reference to whom? With reference to Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka.
In regard to what matter?
Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife; this was the case.
Is there therein a formal rule (*paññatti*), a supplementary rule (*anupaññatti*), and a rule for an unarisen offense (*anuppannapaññatti*)?
There is one formal rule and two supplementary rules.
There is no "proclamation concerning what has not yet arisen" in that [category].
Is it a proclamation for all cases or a proclamation for specific cases?
It is a proclamation for all cases.
Is it a common designation or an uncommon designation?
It is a common designation.
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
A rule prescribed for both [monks and nuns].
In which of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha is it included, and where does it belong?
It is included in the Nidāna and belongs to the Nidāna.
By which summary does it come under a summary?
It comes under the second summary.
Of the four failures, which failure is it?
Failure in virtue.
Among the seven classes of offenses, to which class does it belong?
It belongs to the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika).
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
It originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, but not from speech ... [and so on].
By whom were they brought? They were brought down in succession:
Upāli and Dāsaka.
Soṇaka and Siggava,
with Moggaliputta as the fifth—
these [five] were in the land called Jambusiri.
... [as before] ... These Nāgas possess great wisdom;
they know the Vinaya and are skilled in the path.
"The Tambapaṇṇiya [monks] proclaimed the Vinaya Piṭaka on the island.

Regarding that which was established as a *pārājika* offense by the Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—on account of taking what is not given: where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom? With reference to Dhaniya, the potter’s son.
In what matter? Dhaniya, the potter’s son, took wood that had not been given by the king; it was in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti) and one supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins:
it may originate from both body and mind, but not from speech;
it may originate from both speech and mind, but not from the body.
It may originate from body, speech, and mind ... [as before] ...
On account of intentionally depriving a human being of life, where was the *pārājika* offense laid down?
It was laid down at Vesālī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a number of bhikkhus.
On account of what matter?
A number of bhikkhus took the lives of one another; this was the case.
There is one primary rule (paññatti) and one supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins: [the origin of action, the origin of speech, and the origin of both].
It may originate from both body and mind, but not from speech;
it may originate from both speech and mind, but not from the body;
it may originate from body, speech, and mind... [and so forth].
Where was the offense of defeat (pārājika) prescribed for the purpose of boasting about a non-existent, unreal superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma)?
It was prescribed at Vesālī.
With reference to whom was it prescribed?
Concerning the monks dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā River.
On what matter? On this matter:
the monks dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā River spoke in praise of one another’s superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) to householders; it was on that matter.
There is one original rule (paññatti) and one subsequent rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins:
it may originate from both body and mind, but not from speech.
It may originate from speech and mind, but not from body;
it may originate from body, speech, and mind …pe….
The four *pārājika* rules are concluded.
2. The Section on Saṅghādisesa, etc.

By the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—where was the Saṅghādisesa offense prescribed for the intentional emission of semen? With reference to whom? On account of what matter?
…pe… And by whom was it brought forth?
Where was this Saṅghādisesa rule laid down by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—concerning the intentional emission of semen?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the Venerable Seyyasaka.
On what basis? On the basis that the Venerable Seyyasaka, having made an effort, discharged semen; on that basis.
Is there therein a rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), and a rule for what has not yet arisen (anuppannapaññatti)?
There is one rule and one supplementary rule;
there is no rule for what has not yet arisen therein.
Is it a rule of universal application or a rule of partial application?
It is a rule of universal application.
Is it a common rule or an uncommon rule?
Is it an uncommon designation?
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
It is a designation from one side.
In which of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha is it included, and in what is it contained?
It is included in the Introduction (Nidāna) and contained within the Introduction.
By which recitation does it come into the recitation?
It comes under the third summary.
Of the four failures, which failure is it?
It is failure in virtue.
Of the seven classes of offenses, which class of offense is it? It is the class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Sangha (saṅghādisesa).
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
It originates from one origination:
it originates from both body and mind, not from speech ... [as before] ...
From whom was it brought?
Handed down in succession:
Upāli, Dāsaka,
and likewise Soṇaka and Siggava.
With Moggaliputta as the fifth,
these [councils] took place in the land called Jambusiri.
…pe…
These Nāgas of great wisdom,
knowers of the Vinaya and skilled in the Path,
proclaimed the Vinaya on the Island.
"The Piṭaka of Tambapaṇṇi.
Where was the Saṅghādisesa rule concerning physical contact with a woman established?
It was established at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Udāyī.
On what basis?
The Venerable Udāyī committed physical contact with a woman; this is the case.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin—namely, intentional action.
It originates from both body and mind,
not from speech … [as before] … Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense concerning the addressing of a woman with indecent words laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Udāyī.
On account of what matter?
The Venerable Udāyī addressed a woman with indecent words; this is the basis for the offense.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins: [namely,] from body, from speech, and from both body and speech.
It may originate from both body and mind, but not from speech;
it may originate from both speech and mind, but not from body;
it may originate from body, speech, and mind... [and so on].
Where was the Saṅghādisesa rule regarding speaking in praise of serving one’s own desires in the presence of a woman laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the Venerable Udāyī.
On what basis? On the basis that the Venerable Udāyī spoke in praise of serving one's own desires in the presence of a woman; on that basis.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins ... [etc.
... On account of engaging in matchmaking, where was the Saṅghādisesa offense prescribed?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Udāyī.
In what matter? Venerable Udāyī engaged in matchmaking; it was in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti) and one supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates through six origins:

it may originate from the body, not from speech or mind; it may originate from speech, not from body or mind; [it may originate from the mind, not from body or speech; it may originate from body and speech, not from mind; it may originate from body and mind, not from speech; it may originate from speech and mind, not from body].
It may arise from both body and speech, but not from mind;
it may arise from both body and mind, but not from speech;
it may arise from both speech and mind, but not from body.
It may originate from body, speech, and mind … [as before] … Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense concerning having a hut built by means of begging formulated?
It was formulated at Āḷavī.
Concerning whom?
Concerning the monks of Āḷavī.
On what matter?
The monks of Āḷavī had huts built by means of solicitation; this is the case.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
It originates from six origins of offenses; it originates through all six origins … [and so forth].
Where was the Saṅghādisesa rule concerning the building of a large dwelling laid down?
It was laid down at Kosambī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the Venerable Channa.
"In what matter?
In the matter of the Venerable Channa clearing the site for a dwelling by having a certain sacred tree cut down.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
It originates from six origins of offenses through six origins [of action] ...
[as before] ... In what place was the Saṅghādisesa offense prescribed for the reason of groundlessly accusing a bhikkhu of an offense entailing defeat (pārājika)?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom? With reference to the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka.
In what matter? The monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka groundlessly accused the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta of an offense involving defeat; that was the matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins ... [as above] ...

On account of what cause was the Saṅghādisesa offense established for a monk who, by taking some minor point or pretext from a legal issue belonging to one category, accuses another of an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika)?
It was established at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom? With reference to the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka.
On account of what matter?

The monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, on account of a certain part and a mere pretext of a legal issue belonging to one category, accused the venerable Dabba Mallaputta of an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*) concerning that matter. There is one formal rule (*paññatti*). Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [as before] … *Note: The phrase "ekā paññatti" refers to the specific rule established by the Buddha regarding this case.

The term "channaṁ āpattisamuṭṭhānānaṁ tīhi samuṭṭhānehi samuṭṭhāti" indicates that among the six ways offenses arise (through body, speech, mind, body and speech, body and mind, speech and mind), this offense arises through three: body, speech, and body and speech.*
Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense concerning a monk who causes a schism in the Saṅgha, due to his failure to desist after being exhorted up to three times, laid down?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom?
Concerning Devadatta. On what basis?
On the basis of Devadatta’s attempt to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṅgha. On that basis.
There is one classification.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin—it originates from body, speech, and mind. …pe…
Where was the Saṅghādisesa rule laid down on account of the non-renunciation [of a course] following the exhortation up to the third time of monks who are schismatics and followers of schismatics?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom?
Concerning a number of bhikkhus.
On what matter? On that matter concerning which a number of bhikkhus became followers and partisans of Devadatta as he was striving for a schism in the Saṅgha; on that matter.
There is one classification.
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin—it originates from body, speech, and mind. …pe…
Where was the Saṅghādisesa rule concerning a bhikkhu who is difficult to speak with, on account of not desisting after being exhorted up to three times, laid down?
It was laid down at Kosambī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the Venerable Channa.
On what matter?
On the matter that the Venerable Channa, when being addressed by the monks in accordance with the Dhamma, made himself one who should not be spoken to; on that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin—it originates from body, speech, and mind. …pe…
Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense formulated on account of a monk who does not desist after being admonished up to three times for corrupting families?
It was formulated at Sāvatthī. With reference to whom?
With reference to Devadatta.
Concerning the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka. On what basis?

On the basis that the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka, having been subjected by the Saṅgha to an act of banishment, caused [the monks] to fall into favoritism, ill-will, delusion, and fear regarding those who were evil. It was on this basis.
There is one classification.
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from body, speech, and mind. …pe…
In reference to whom was the *dukkaṭa* offense prescribed for discharging feces, urine, or spittle into water out of disrespect?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the group of six bhikkhus. On what basis?
On the basis that the group of six bhikkhus discharged feces, urine, and spittle into water. On that basis.
One is a primary rule (paññatti); one is a secondary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, but not from speech ... [and so on].
The first section, the Chapter on the Formulation of Rules Regarding Wood, is finished.
